title_th: การสั่งอาหารริมทาง
recycles: yes/no answers with a short reason ("No bag, thanks")
register: Casual-friendly, fast and transactional — short phrases, first-name-free, no honorifics; politeness carried by "please/thanks", not by long sentences

targets.why_it_matters_here: The vendor says the total once, over a noisy street, and you pay immediately. If your "fifteen" sounds like "fifty" when you repeat it back, you hand over the wrong money or argue about a price you actually agreed to — and if you hear order number "thirty-four" as "forty-three" you stand there while your food goes cold on the counter.

Street-food orders are one or two words long, so the final consonant carries the whole meaning. Drop the /s/ in "rice" and the vendor hears "rye"; drop the /g/ in "egg" and nothing gets added; say "pork" without the /k/ and you get pointed at the wrong tray. There is no second sentence to repair it — the vendor is already cooking.

model_dialogues.label: A2 — One order at a noodle stall (everything goes to plan)

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.text: Hi there! What can I get you?
lines.th: หวัดดีครับ! รับอะไรดีครับ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: One pad thai, please.

lines.speaker: Vendor

lines.text: No worries. Eat in or takeaway?

lines.th: ใส่กล่องกลับ เพิ่มไข่ได้ไหม

lines.text: Sure. That's eight fifty altogether.
lines.th: ได้ รวมแปดเหรียญห้าสิบ

model_dialogues.label: B1 — Same stall, but sold out, mild "medium", a card surcharge and a call-out number

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.text: G'day! You right to order?
lines.th: หวัดดี! พร้อมสั่งยัง

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Yes. Two chicken skewers, please.
lines.th: พร้อมแล้ว ขอไก่ปิ้งสองไม้

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.text: Sorry, chicken's sold out. I've got pork or tofu.
lines.th: โทษที ไก่หมดแล้ว เหลือหมูกับเต้าหู้

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Pork, then. Two pork skewers.
lines.th: งั้นเอาหมู หมูปิ้งสองไม้

lines.text: Sweet. How spicy — mild, medium, or hot?
lines.th: โอเค เอาเผ็ดแค่ไหน เผ็ดน้อย กลาง หรือเผ็ดมาก

lines.speaker: Customer

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Okay. Can you make it spicier?
lines.th: งั้นทำให้เผ็ดขึ้นอีกหน่อยได้ไหม

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.text: Will do. Anything else? Rice is two fifty extra.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: One rice, and a cold water.

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.text: Righto. That comes to fifteen fifty.
lines.th: ได้เลย ทั้งหมดสิบห้าเหรียญห้าสิบ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Sorry, fifteen fifty or fifty fifteen?

lines.speaker: Vendor
lines.text: Fifteen dollars fifty. One, five, point five zero.
lines.th: สิบห้าเหรียญห้าสิบ หนึ่ง-ห้า จุด ห้า-ศูนย์

lines.speaker: Customer

lines.speaker: Vendor

chunk_drills.label: Placing the order (quantity + item)
examples: Can I get three spring rolls, please?
One rice and a cold water, please.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles numbers 1-20 and plural -s; the plural /s/ and /z/ is itself a final-consonant target (skewers, rolls, noodles).

chunk_drills.label: Setting the spice level
chunk_drills.pattern: Not too [adjective], please. / Can you make it [comparative]? / No [ingredient], please.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Comparative -er (spicier, hotter) recycled from describing preferences; 'not too + adj' as a softener.

chunk_drills.label: Extras and swaps
chunk_drills.pattern: Can I add [a/an + item]? / With extra [item]. / Without [item].
examples: Can I swap the chicken for tofu?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: a/an before vowel sounds (an egg); recycles 'with/without' from café ordering.

chunk_drills.label: Eat in or takeaway
chunk_drills.pattern: Takeaway, please. / Eat in, thanks. / No bag, thanks.
examples: Can I have a fork, please?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: One-chunk answers to a two-option question — recycles short-answer strategy from shop and café units.

chunk_drills.label: Price, checking and repair
chunk_drills.pattern: How much is [item]? / How much altogether? / Sorry, was that [number] or [number]?
examples: How much is the pad thai?
Sorry, was that fifteen or fifty?
Sorry, could you say that again?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles 'How much…?' and price numbers; adds the 'X or Y?' repair question used across all transaction units.

chunk_drills.label: Waiting and collecting
chunk_drills.pattern: How long is the wait? / What number am I? / Did you say [number]?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles time expressions (about ten minutes) and the teen/ty number contrast.

guided_roleplay.learner_role: You are hungry at a busy night-market food stall. Order one main dish with the spice level you actually want, add one extra, check the price, and find out when it's ready.
flow: Step 1 — Open: greet and order. "Hi. One pad thai, please."
Step 2 — Spice level: answer the vendor's question with a clear level. "Not too spicy, please."
Step 3 — Extras: add or remove one thing. "Can I add an egg?" / "No peanuts, please."
Step 4 — Eat in or takeaway: choose one. "Takeaway, please."
Step 5 — Money: ask the total and repeat the number back. "How much altogether?" → "Eight fifty?"
Step 6 — Pay: cash or card, and refuse or accept a bag. "Card, please. No bag, thanks."
Step 7 — Collect: ask about the wait and your number. "How long is the wait?" → "Thirty-four, not forty-three?"

free_roleplay.ai_persona: A friendly, fast-talking street-food vendor at a packed evening market. Speaks in short chunks, uses casual fillers ('no worries', 'righto', 'you right?'), talks over sizzling noise, and never waits long for an answer. Warm but efficient — repeats things if asked, but only if asked.
free_roleplay.a2_behavior: Sticks to the standard sequence: takes the order, asks spice level, asks eat in or takeaway, states one clear total, takes payment, gives an order number. Uses simple numbers under twenty and confirms the learner's repeat-back.
b1_curveballs: The item the learner wants is sold out — offers two alternatives and asks them to choose quickly.
Says the total fast and unclearly ('fifteen fifty'), then tests whether the learner repeats it back correctly.
Warns that 'medium' at this stall is much hotter (or much milder) than expected and asks the learner to decide again.
Cash only, or a card surcharge for orders under twenty — the learner must react and still pay.
Charges extra for rice, sauce or a bag, so the total goes up after the learner already heard a price.
Calls a number that sounds like the learner's ('forty-three' vs 'thirty-four') and lets them almost take the wrong order.
Asks a question the learner didn't prepare: 'Anything to drink?' or 'You want it cut up?'

roleplay_rubric.criterion: Ordered a specific item with a quantity, audibly (number + item + please)
Stated a spice level or asked for it to be changed ('not too spicy' / 'a bit spicier')
Handled the money step: asked the total and repeated the number back before paying
Chose takeaway or eat in and dealt with the extras question (bag / drink / extra rice)
Used at least one repair phrase when unsure ('Sorry, was that fifteen or fifty?' / 'Could you say that again?')
Pronunciation: teen/ty numbers distinct, and final consonants audible in rice, pork, egg, bag, cash
Register stayed short and casual-friendly — 'please/thanks' rather than long formal sentences
Coped with an off-script curveball (sold out, surcharge, wrong number called) and still finished the order

register_culture_note.en: Street-food ordering is the fastest register in this course. Vendors want the shortest usable answer: 'Two pork skewers, please' — not 'Excuse me sir, I would like to order two pieces of pork.' Politeness lives in one word: please, thanks, cheers. Being brief is not rude here; being slow is what causes stress, because there's a queue behind you. Decide before you reach the counter, then say your order in one breath. The two things you must say clearly are the number and the last sound of the food word — that's what the vendor actually listens for.

do_dont.avoid: Saying "ri-" with no /s/ so it sounds like "rye"
do_dont.prefer: "Rice" — let the /s/ finish before you stop

do_dont.avoid: Nodding when you didn't catch the price
"Egg" said as "eh" — the extra never gets added
do_dont.prefer: "Can I add an egg?" with the /g/ landing

register_culture_note.thai_cultural_note: Two habits from Thai markets don't travel. First, haggling: at street stalls and food trucks outside Thailand prices are fixed and posted, and asking for a discount reads as odd rather than friendly. Second, pointing-and-nodding: in Thailand you can often just point at the tray and hold up fingers, and the vendor sorts it out. Abroad the vendor usually can't see the food from where you stand and will ask spice level, size, extras and payment out loud — so you have to speak. Also, saying a plain 'Two skewers, please' with no softening is completely normal and not impolite; you do not need an apology before every request.

can_do_checkpoints.statement: I can order a specific dish with a quantity at a street-food stall.
I can say the spice level I want, including 'not too spicy'.
I can choose takeaway or eat in and add one extra, like an egg.
I can ask the total, repeat the price back, and pay by cash or card.
I can react when my dish is sold out and choose an alternative on the spot.
I can handle an unexpected extra charge (bag, rice, card surcharge) and confirm the new total.
I can check my order number and ask how long the wait is.
My teen/ty numbers are distinguishable and my final consonants (rice, pork, egg, bag, cash) are audible over street noise.
